item.title: Is the business of frontier AI companies selling tokens? Value capture and equity prices
item.description: arXiv:2610.14145v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine business models that could support frontier AI companies' valuations and the public evidence of plans to earn income beyond selling model access. Reverse cash-flow calculations for OpenAI and Anthropic yield combined year-ten revenue requirements of \$2.79 trillion or \$733 billion, depending on financial assumptions. Public documents identify proposed payments and ownership interests that could supply additional income, such as through partnerships on pharmaceuticals, robotics, or materials science. We discuss how these arrangements relate to firm boundaries and value capture.
item.dc:creator: Andrew J. Peterson

item.title: Safety Research and the Allocation of Frontier Compute
item.description: arXiv:2610.14305v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Who should give up compute for AI safety research: customers or capability research? Safety paid for by customers delays no capability. Safety paid for by research slows the frontier, which gives knowledge more time to accumulate but postpones what a finished frontier provides. In a frontier-takeoff model, the cheaper source at a given allocation is set by a threshold in demand capacity. Demand capacity is the share of compute customers can use once the frontier is finished. Research should pay too only when demand capacity lies below the threshold. Where the threshold sits depends on how fast the value of customer services diminishes. In the calibration it rises with the service budget, because each further unit taken from customers costs them more. Safety paid for by customers should come early: its ratio to customer compute falls over the takeoff unless safety productivity rises fast. In a calibration with a tight service budget, early customer-funded safety lowers the probability of catastrophe from 75 to 51 percent. That is within one point of the best rule found that may also slow research.
item.dc:creator: Li Gan

item.title: Pregnancy and Interrupted Schooling: Evidence from Monthly Histories
item.description: arXiv:2610.14317v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pregnancy can disrupt schooling before infant care begins. We use monthly histories from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1997 to study school interruptions during pregnancy and after childbirth and whether students later return to school or earn a diploma or GED. We jointly model conception and sustained interruptions in enrollment, allowing persistent unobserved differences to affect both processes. Under the timing-of-events identifying assumptions, pregnancy raises the monthly interruption rate to nearly four times the rate without pregnancy. Interruption rates are elevated before delivery and remain elevated afterward. After an interruption, students already exposed to pregnancy return to school and earn a diploma or GED less often within two years. These findings show that schooling disruption is already present during pregnancy, before the additional demands of infant care begin.
item.dc:creator: Jonghoon Park, R. Alan Seals

item.title: From Observation to Intervention: Mastering Bus Holding Control from Historical Uncontrolled Trajectories with Offline Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.14632v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bus operations are inherently unstable---buses initially dispatched at equal headways will inevitably end up bunching up. This issue exacerbates passenger waiting times, creates load imbalances between buses, and undermines service reliability. Reinforcement learning (RL) has proven highly effective for mitigating bus bunching and outperforms traditional model-based approaches. However, existing RL approaches require agents to continuously interact with the environment, which potentially disrupts the bus system before effective policies are learned. This paper proposes an Offline Graph-based Multi-agent Actor-Critic (Offline-GMAC) method that trains bus holding policies using only readily available logged GPS data collected during normal uncontrolled operations, thereby eliminating the need for disruptive online interaction or exploration. The method employs general graph neural networks for multi-agent credit assignment. A key innovation of our method is a data augmentation scheme that synthesizes unperformed holding actions from historical uncontrolled bus trajectories. The scheme exploits the equivalence between stochastic link travel time delays and deliberate holding interventions. Under mild assumptions, we prove that the 1-Wasserstein distance between synthesized and target state transition distributions is bounded above by a term that scales linearly with the standard deviation of link travel times plus a tunable synthesis-dependent term. Evaluations using real-world bus data demonstrate that the proposed offline method achieves performance comparable to, and in some cases, even better than its online counterpart.
item.dc:creator: Minyu Shen, Xiaowen Bi, Weihua Gu, Zhandong Xu, Yuezhong Wu, Feng Xiao, Lu Li

item.title: Displacement Is Endogenous: AI Workers in a Search-and-Matching Labor Market
item.description: arXiv:2610.14850v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We build a labor market in which AI systems enter as workers: they apply for jobs, pass screenings, get hired, and get dismissed, alongside humans. Firms post vacancies, workers search with friction, and product demand slopes downward. Across 30 seeded runs per configuration, AI entry at 70% of the human wage raises unemployment by 4.1 percentage points (95% CI 3.5 to 4.6) and leaves 12.2 fewer humans employed (CI 10.5 to 13.9). Layoffs dominate when AI is much cheaper than humans: the layoff margin accounts for 7.2 of the lost jobs and reduced hiring for 5.0, though most dismissed workers find work again. A wider price gap reduces displacement, because cheap AI makes firms expand: at price parity, with zero dismissals, the unemployment effect is largest at 9.2 points (CI 8.6 to 9.9), all of it through hiring. That parity result survives cutting AI applications from five per period to one. Demand elasticity decides how many workers AI displaces. Screening changes who gets hired and leaves the displacement total unchanged.
item.dc:creator: Ibrahim Denis Fofanah (Pace University, New York, NY, USA)

item.title: Too Late to Prune: Generative AI, the Screen, and Team Creative Decisions
item.description: arXiv:2610.14984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative AI makes options cheap and shifts the bottleneck of creative work from generating options to screening them. We argue that AI's value depends on whether its options arrive before or after the team's screen. In our model, early options compete for a place in the portfolio; late options arrive after that competition and are kept unscreened. In a preregistered experiment, we randomly assigned 148 three-person teams to five schedules of access to the same language model during a product-design task with timed search and selection stages. Moving the same 15 minutes of access from search to selection lowered expert-rated creativity by 0.62 standard deviations, although teams used the model at similar rates. Platform logs locate the difference at the screen. Early access enlarged the pool of ideas fivefold, and teams pruned it. Late-access teams reached the screen with the same small pool as teams without AI and then searched again, devoting 29% of their selection-stage queries to generating new options, compared with 11% for teams with access throughout. Late access added breadth, not quality: these teams submitted 73% more proposals than did teams without AI. Language-model judges detected the benefit of access but not the cost of late timing.
item.dc:creator: Difang Huang, Shumin Yu, Fadong Chen, Weihua Zhou

item.title: AI Advice Reinforces Traditional Gender Roles
item.description: arXiv:2610.14036v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Professionals are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence (AI) for career advice. We tested whether large language models (LLMs) provide different advice to female and male job candidates in the context of career negotiations. Across two large-scale audit experiments, including four leading models, the LLMs not only recommended lower salary targets for female than male personas, but also constructed distinct negotiation agendas, prioritizing flexibility, caregiving, and well-being more highly for female candidates, and financial rewards, mobility, and advancement more highly for male candidates. These differences closely tracked independent human ratings of employment terms associated with primary caregiver and breadwinner roles, respectively. Our findings identify a subtle pathway through which personalized AI advice may reinforce gender inequality at work: steering otherwise equivalent users toward traditional gender roles.
item.dc:creator: Nadja Born, Jared R. Curhan, Hannah Riley Bowles

item.title: Allocative Efficiency and the Returns to Innovation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14969v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When producers in a network compete in quantities, an innovator's profit contains none of the change in allocative efficiency that its innovation causes, whether a gain or a loss, because its own choices are optimal and other effects on its profit are transfers. A process innovator also forgoes its own and downstream markups on the output its innovation adds at a fixed allocation, worth 14 to 26 percent of its cost saving for U.S. public firms in 2015. For innovators accounting for 68 percent of sales, the change in allocative efficiency exceeds a tenth of the private return. In a Markov R&D game, reallocation of R&D across firms is likewise external to the innovator. Rivals' profits and market values can misstate the welfare cost of business stealing from them even in sign. With estimated spillovers, the social return to R&D is 5.39 times the private return, against 2.53 in output-based accounting with estimated business stealing, mainly because that accounting credits the innovator with its rivals' lost sales.
item.dc:creator: Koki Okumura

item.title: The Buffett Effect
item.description: arXiv:2610.17231v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study whether stock disclosures by recognizable investors generate abnormal market reactions beyond the reactions produced by comparable but non-recognizable managers. We define the Buffett effect as the incremental abnormal return to a disclosed new position that is attributable to the public recognition of the disclosing investor. We construct a recognition index from Wikipedia pageviews and ProQuest news mentions. Using data from 2000 to 2025 we compare market reaction to disclosures of 24 recognizable discretionary funds with disclosures of 24 matched control funds. New-position disclosures by recognizable managers generate a positive disclosure premium over the filing date and the following trading days, and the premium increases with investor recognition. We construct calendar-time portfolios that mechanically copy each group's disclosed purchases and find that copying the most recognized investors earns a significant alpha that persists for months and does not reverse. The evidence is most consistent with an entangled attention-information channel: investor recognition directs scarce investor attention toward selected disclosures, and the information revealed in those disclosures is then capitalized into prices.
item.dc:creator: Pawel Robert Smolinski, Siddharth Saridevi

item.title: Media Slant is Contagious
item.description: arXiv:2202.07269v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper examines the diffusion of media slant. We document the influence of Fox News Channel (FNC) on the partisan slant of local newspapers in the U.S. over the years 1995-2008. We measure the political slant of local newspapers by scaling the news article texts to Republicans' and Democrats' speeches in Congress. Using channel positioning as an instrument for viewership, we find that higher FNC viewership causes local newspapers to adopt more right-wing slant. The effect emerges gradually, only several years after FNC's introduction, mirroring the channel's growing influence on voting behaviour. A main driver of the shift in newspaper slant appears to be a change in local political preferences.
item.dc:creator: Philine Widmer, Cl\'ementine Abed Meraim, Sergio Galletta, Elliott Ash

item.title: Extracurricular Exercise and Academic Achievement: Evidence from the China Education Panel Survey
item.description: arXiv:2312.11484v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Does physical exercise enhance adolescent academic achievement, and is there an optimal daily duration? Linking two waves of the China Education Panel Survey ($N=8,247$), we examine this association using restricted cubic splines and classroom fixed effects. Prospective estimates without prior-score controls place non-exercising students 0.162 mean subject-z units below peers exercising one hour daily. Flexible baseline-achievement controls shrink this shortfall by 85.1 percent to 0.024. The exercise block is not jointly significant ($p=0.301$), and curvature tests fail to reject linearity ($p=0.659$). Subgroup estimates yield similar gender profiles, with stronger evidence of location variation in English. These findings establish the importance of academic history in observed exercise gradients and challenge prescriptive exercise targets derived from fitted observational turning points.
item.dc:creator: Ningyi Li

item.title: Agentic Workflows for Economic Research: Design, Implementation, and Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2504.09736v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can now assist across the economic research lifecycle, yet general-purpose LLMs and agent systems give no assurance that their outputs meet the discipline's bar. We present an agentic-workflow methodology that carries a research question through the full lifecycle, from ideation and literature review through modeling, data, implementation, estimation, and reporting, across seven specialized teams under a cross-team orchestrator, with human-in-the-loop review at each stage. The methodology incorporates two commitments. The first, trustworthy execution, is a shared infrastructure that verifies outputs, records the provenance of every step, bounds each agent's authority, addresses agent-specific threats, and serves every LLM locally on open weights. The second, reasoning as an economist, makes disciplinary checks explicit in the workflow: agents state identification strategies for causal claims, check structural models against stylized facts by simulation, and search for counterexamples to theoretical claims. Together they produce a first research prototype in hours, with every step's provenance and verification verdict recorded. A two-tier framework evaluates the workflows across fourteen dimensions, combining execution-log metrics with a dual-judge LLM-as-reviewer ensemble across all seven teams.
item.dc:creator: Herbert Dawid, Philipp Harting, Hankui Wang, Zhongli Wang, Jiachen Yi

item.title: Are Higher Suspicious Transaction Report Volumes Associated with More Future Money-Laundering Convictions?
item.description: arXiv:2508.18932v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Almost all countries require banks to file suspicious transaction reports (STRs) to help authorities detect and prosecute money laundering. The number of STRs filed in a country is an often-cited metric in international anti-money laundering (AML) compliance evaluations. However, it remains unclear if the volume of STRs filed in a country is associated with the country's future number of money laundering convictions. Using data from Europol, the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, and the European Sourcebook of Crime and Criminal Justice Statistics, we examine if STR volumes can be associated with future money-laundering conviction volumes in countries in the European Union. Our analysis employs pooled and fixed-effects regression models with one- to five-year lags, controlling for population sizes, shadow-economy estimates, and police force sizes. In our pooled and country-specific fixed-effects models, STR volumes appear to be positively associated with future convictions. However, the association weakens and becomes insignificant when we control for both country-specific and common time effects. Our results provide a caution against assuming that STR volumes, by themselves, are reliable indicators of future money-laundering convictions and, to the extent convictions reflect outcomes, AML effectiveness.
item.dc:creator: Rasmus Ingemann Tuffveson Jensen, Sebastian Holmby Hansen, Kalle Johannes Rose

item.title: Playing Against the Machine: Cooperation, Communication, and Strategy Heterogeneity in Repeated Prisoner's Dilemma
item.description: arXiv:2603.15852v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper investigates how natural language communication with an AI agent affects human cooperative behaviour in indefinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma games. We conduct a laboratory experiment (n = 126) with two between-subjects treatments varying whether human participants chat with an AI chatbot (GPT-5.2) before every round or only before the first round of each supergame, and benchmark against human-human data from Dvorak and Fehrler (2024) (n = 108). We find four main results. First, cooperation against the AI is high and initially comparable to human-human levels, but unlike in the human-human setting, where cooperation converges to near-complete levels, cooperation against the AI plateaus and never reaches full cooperation. Second, repeated communication, which substantially increases cooperation in human-human interactions, has no detectable effect in the human-AI setting. Third, strategy estimation reveals that human-AI subjects favour Grim Trigger under pre-play communication and remain dispersed under repeated communication, whereas human-human subjects converge to Tit-for-Tat and unconditional cooperation respectively. Fourth, human-AI conversations contain more explicit strategy commitments but fewer emotional and social messages. These results suggest that humans cooperate with AI at high rates but do not develop the trust observed in human-human interactions. Cooperation in the human-AI setting is sustained through conditional rules rather than through the social bonds and mutual understanding that characterise human-human cooperation.
item.dc:creator: Chowdhury Mohammad Sakib Anwar, Konstantinos Georgalos

item.title: Conditional Disclosure as a Coordination Device
item.description: arXiv:2604.00874v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: People with controversial views may stay silent rather than speak out alone, though in a large enough group they could speak safely together. A Social Assurance Contract makes disclosure conditional: signed commitments of support stay private until enough people have signed for it to be safe to publish. In contrast, a survey can measure hidden support but does not make identification conditional on enough others joining. I derive the contract's exact advantage over speaking openly, and when that advantage disappears. Such contracts can turn a few people who would speak alone into a larger coalition.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Cashman

item.title: Global Automation Atlas
item.description: arXiv:2605.17086v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Automation can displace or complement labour, but this need not be constant across economies. Existing exposure measures typically assign fixed scores to tasks or occupations and capture cross-country variation through employment structure. We posit that exposure to automation depends jointly on task content and country-level conditions. We use a large language model to classify 18,797 work tasks in 124 economies by exposure, labour margin, technology channel and artificial-intelligence materiality. Country conditioning changes the classification of the same task and the occupation exposure rankings, especially in lower-income economies. Country-conditioned scores improve out-of-country predictions of firms' production-technology use and AI adoption; physical-execution exposure tracks industrial-robot use and density, while Atlas scores align with observed work-related ChatGPT and Claude use across activities and countries. The share of tasks exposed to automation ranges from 3.3% to 61.6% across countries. It rises with income but varies considerably within income groups. Lower-income economies are more concentrated in rule-based and labour-substituting forms of automation, whereas physical execution, planning and inference channels, together with labour-augmenting uses of artificial intelligence, become more prominent with development. Combined with employment data, we find that women are disproportionately employed in occupations with substitution-facing exposure. Across countries, higher informality is associated with a smaller exposed-task share but a larger substitution-only share among exposed tasks. Machine-learning hypothesis generation methods point to both economic and institutional drivers: automation is more feasible where firms have machinery, digital records and connected systems, but less so where tasks depend on local knowledge and trusted relationships.
item.dc:creator: Prashant Garg, Tommaso Crosta, Jasmin Baier

item.title: Decomposing Wage Stagnation: Employment Reallocation, Wage Structure,and Demographics
item.description: arXiv:2607.01561v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Japan's average log real hourly wages rose from the 1980s to the mid-1990s, declined through the mid-2010s, and partially recovered thereafter. This paper decomposes these changes from 1980 to 2024 into four components: demographic change across worker types, employment reallocation across job types, changes in relative wage structure across job types, and unweighted mean wage growth. The first two represent different margins of adjustment in employment, while the latter two represent different margins of adjustment in wages. The framework combines a shift-share decomposition across worker types with an augmented Olley-Pakes decomposition across job types within worker types. Employment reallocation reflects changes in employment shares across job types, whereas changes in relative wage structure reflect changes in average log wages within job types that alter wage differences across job types. The contributions of the four components vary across periods. Before 1996, unweighted mean wage growth and changes in relative wage structure contribute positively, while demographic change and employment reallocation contribute negatively. During the 1996-2014 period, unweighted mean wage growth and changes in relative wage structure turn negative, so that all four components are negative. After 2014, the recovery mainly reflects unweighted mean wage growth. The contributions from employment reallocation and changes in relative wage structure differ not only between full-time and part-time jobs but also across establishment sizes and industries within employment type. The paper uses the same framework to decompose changes in Japan's gender wage gap.
item.dc:creator: Ken Yamada

item.title: Does the Gender Wage Gap Originate at Labor Market Entry? Evidence from South Korea
item.description: arXiv:2608.03153v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When in the lifecycle does a large gender wage gap emerge? South Korea has the largest aggregate gender pay gap (29%) in the OECD. Among recent college graduates the conditional gap is only 3.3% over 2008-2019, falling from 3.4% to 2.5%. Correcting for differential selection into employment with semiparametric and machine learning methods leaves it unchanged. Nonparametric and semiparametric bounds contain the point estimates. Selection-corrected quantile regression shows that the remaining entry-level gap is concentrated at the top of the distribution. In Korean panel data the corrected gap widens severalfold across the prime-age workforce, where the selection correction becomes first order. Korea's gender wage disparity is mostly generated after labor market entry.
item.dc:creator: Dongwoo Kim

item.title: Optimal Transport in Economics
item.description: arXiv:2609.06277v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Optimal transport provides a common language for allocation, equilibrium, computation, and inference. Its primal problem assigns mass or agents, while its dual variables admit economic interpretations as utilities, prices, and scarcity rents. This review explains why this combination has proved unusually effective in economics. We first present the core results, including Kantorovich duality, integrality, cyclical monotonicity, the canonical distance and quadratic costs, and entropic regularization. We then trace the field's development from planning and operations research to modern analysis, statistics, and computation. The economic literature is organized around two roles for transport: as a model of matching, trade, hedonic equilibrium, and aggregate assignment; and as a tool for coupling distributions, measuring discrepancies, constructing multivariate ranks, solving inverse problems, and certifying economic conclusions. We conclude by examining extensions beyond transferable utility, one-to-one matching, static allocation, and unconstrained transport, together with open questions involving learning and identification across multiple markets.
item.dc:creator: Amine Fahli, Alfred Galichon

item.title: The Myth of Restrictive Working-Time Agreements: Firms' Working-Time Adjustment after Exit from Collective Bargaining
item.description: arXiv:2610.12049v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Employers in Germany argue that collective agreements restrict their flexibility concerning working hours. Using data from the IAB Establishment Panel for the years 2008 to 2024, we investigate working-time adjustments after exit from collective bargaining. We find that exit is associated with only a modest increase in weekly working hours of around 0.3 to 0.6 per cent using fixed-effects and event-study models, corresponding to eight to thirteen additional minutes per week. This adjustment occurs shortly after leaving collective bargaining coverage. We further find no evidence that other margins of working-time adjustment, such as Saturday or Sunday work, are used more extensively after exit. In contrast to previous survey evidence, our findings call into question that working-hours constraints are one of the main drivers of exit from collective bargaining coverage.
item.dc:creator: Vinzenz Pyka, Andr\'e Rieder

item.title: Web3 x AI Agents: Landscape, Integrations, and Foundational Challenges
item.description: arXiv:2508.02773v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The convergence of Web3 technologies and AI agents is a rapidly evolving frontier that is reshaping decentralized ecosystems. This paper presents the first comprehensive landscape analysis of the intersection between Web3 and AI agents, examining five critical dimensions: landscape, economics, governance, security, and trust mechanisms. Through an analysis of 979 capitalized Web3-AI agent tokens at a 1 September 2026 cutoff, compared with a cohort of 275 tokens collected at 6 April 2025, we develop a taxonomy and systematically map the current market landscape (RQ1), identifying distinct patterns in project distribution and capitalization. We complement the token frame with on-chain measurement of the agent standards layer: 530,266 ERC-8004 identity registrations across 16 chains and 432,913 x402 settlements on Base. We then investigate four integration domains: AI agents in decentralized finance (RQ2), governance (RQ3), security (RQ4), and Web3 trust mechanisms for agent reliability (RQ5). Infrastructure dominates the landscape in both project count and capitalization; value is highly concentrated (Gini 0.938), and the archived cohort lost 36.4% in capitalization over seventeen months despite token population growth. The agent standards layer shows adoption at scale, but economic throughput remains limited. Across integration domains, AI agents extend DeFi trading and make continuous security auditing affordable, while agents in governance remain largely a blueprint. These findings outline critical considerations for future research toward robust, intelligent, and trustworthy decentralized systems with AI agent interactions.
item.dc:creator: Yiming Shen, Jiashuo Zhang, Zhenzhe Shao, Wenxuan Luo, Yanlin Wang, Ting Chen, Lingfeng Bao, Jiachi Chen

item.title: Neural Evidence and Behavioural Welfare Economics: When Can Neuroeconomics Inform Policy?
item.description: arXiv:2511.19548v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neuroeconomics appears to offer welfare economics an evidential supplement, since neural data may help distinguish choices that express genuine preferences from choices distorted by addiction, framing or self-control failure. This paper asks when such evidence can legitimately inform welfare judgements for policy. It develops a conceptual framework linking three levels of analysis, namely neural signals, computational decision models and normative welfare criteria. The central argument is that neural data can constrain welfare analysis only under four conditions, covering the validity of the neural measure, the identifiability of the decision model, the explicit statement of the welfare criterion, and the institutional context of any policy use. Applying this framework to addiction, neuromarketing and environmental policy, and working through the United Kingdom's Tobacco and Vapes Act 2026, a major intervention justified without any neural measurement, the paper develops a Neuroeconomic Welfare Inference Checklist for neural evidence. Neural data can improve behavioural welfare economics by clarifying the mechanisms behind choice, and they cannot replace normative argument about what counts as welfare. The same reasoning applies to artificial agents trained on human feedback, whose internal reward signals are computational quantities and not welfare measures.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: UCL Journal of Economics, vol. 5 no. 1 (2026)
item.dc:creator: Louis Yiven Zhu

item.title: Measuring Concept Content in Text from LLM Activations: ESG Evidence from Concept Vectors and Linear Probes
item.description: arXiv:2608.07208v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent work shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) encode more information in their activations than they show in their responses. We ask whether the information contained in activations could be used as a source of measurement for the presence of concepts. We compare two algorithms for extraction of concepts, i.e., Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm and linear probing against an embedding baseline, surface baselines, and the model's own response using a human-annotated Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) dataset of financial texts. The best linear probe ranges from 0.6 to 3.3 percentage points below fine-tuned domain classifiers. The probes also outscore the model's own response in all comparisons. Furthermore, the probes outperform the RFM concept vectors in all accuracy comparisons. In a synthetic mixture test, their mean-pooled score tracks the number of concept sentences in a paragraph better than the concept-vector score. Put together, a linear probe on a frozen LLM is a cost-effective and generalizable alternative to fine-tuning a domain classifier.
item.dc:creator: Luc Hazenoot, Zhaochun Ren, Amirhossein Zohrehvand
